sources: Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game

trails.trailTip: This is one of the only maintained, signed trails in the park, reached by floatplane or boat to Port Alsworth — there is no road access anywhere in Lake Clark, so budget travel time and cost for a bush flight before you ever reach the trailhead.
trails.didYouKnow: Port Alsworth, the trail's starting point, is a small floatplane-access community that also serves as the park's headquarters.

trails.trailTip: The maintained trail ends partway up; the final push above treeline is a use-path over loose rock with no markers, so carry a map/GPS and turn back in poor visibility since there is no rescue infrastructure nearby.
trails.didYouKnow: On a clear day the summit offers views of Lake Clark, Six-Mile Lake, and the volcanic peaks of the Chigmit Mountains.

trails.trailTip: A rougher, less-maintained continuation past the Tanalian trails — expect muddy, root-crossed tread and make noise around bends, since dense brush near the lake limits sightlines for bears.
trails.didYouKnow: Kontrashibuna Lake's strikingly clear turquoise color comes from fine glacial sediment ('rock flour') suspended in the water.

trails.trailTip: This is a tidal beach walk, not a built trail — it's only accessible by chartered floatplane onto the beach itself, and coordinating with a guide is strongly recommended since this is one of the park's most concentrated brown bear areas.
trails.didYouKnow: Silver Salmon Creek is renowned for brown bears that dig for clams directly on the open tidal flats at low tide.

trails.trailTip: A historic portage route between interior lakes rather than a graded trail — used mainly by paddlers moving between water bodies, so most visitors will only walk it as part of a longer canoe/kayak trip.
trails.didYouKnow: Portage routes like this one were long used by the Dena'ina people to travel between the region's interconnected lake systems without a boat capable of open water.

trails.trailTip: An unmaintained backcountry route to a remote lake beneath the Chigmit volcanoes — this is true off-trail wilderness travel, so bring navigation tools and file a trip plan since there is no cell coverage and rescue could take days.
trails.didYouKnow: Crescent Lake sits in the shadow of Mount Iliamna, one of two active volcanoes visible from within the park.

trails.trailTip: This historic cross-country travel corridor has no tread, bridges, or markers for most of its length — it is a multi-day wilderness route for experienced backcountry travelers, not a day hike, and river crossings can be dangerous at high water.
trails.didYouKnow: The Telaquana Route follows a traditional Dena'ina travel corridor connecting Lake Clark to the Telaquana Lake area, long used for seasonal subsistence travel.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, all bear viewing on NPS land at Chinitna Bay is confined to two designated viewing areas capped at 15 people each — stick to these marked areas and follow your guide's lead rather than wandering the flats independently.
trails.didYouKnow: Chinitna Bay's tidal salt marsh can host 20 or more brown bears grazing sedge grass at once, one of the densest concentrations of viewable bears in the state.

animals.bestTimeOfDay: Morning / Evening (low tide for beach feeding)
animals.whereToLook: Silver Salmon Creek tidal flats and Chinitna Bay salt marsh
animals.viewingTip: As of September 2026, per NPS.gov, view bears only from the designated viewing areas at Chinitna Bay or from a guide-led position at Silver Salmon Creek, using binoculars or a zoom lens to keep distance — never approach a feeding or fishing bear to get closer.
animals.didYouKnow: Bears here are famous for digging razor clams directly out of the tidal sand at low tide, a foraging behavior rarely seen elsewhere.

animals.whereToLook: Lowland willow flats and wetlands near Port Alsworth
animals.viewingTip: Scan willow-choked wetlands from a distance with binoculars, especially at dawn, and give a cow with calves a wide berth rather than moving closer for a photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Alaska moose are the largest subspecies of moose in the world, with bulls sometimes exceeding 1,500 pounds.

animals.whereToLook: Lakeshores and river mouths near salmon runs
animals.viewingTip: Watch nest trees along the shoreline through binoculars or a spotting scope rather than approaching the base of a nest tree, which can flush an incubating adult.
animals.didYouKnow: Bald eagles congregate in large numbers along Lake Clark's rivers during salmon spawning season, sometimes dozens at a single stretch.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky slopes of the Chigmit Mountains
animals.viewingTip: Spot sheep on distant scree slopes with a spotting scope; their pure white coats stand out against rock, so there's no need to close the distance to see them well.
animals.didYouKnow: Dall sheep rely on nearly vertical terrain to escape predators like wolves and bears, which rarely follow them onto the steepest slopes.

animals.whereToLook: Cook Inlet waters near the park's coastline
animals.viewingTip: Watch for surfacing belugas from shore or a boat with binoculars; Cook Inlet's population is small and endangered, so keep watercraft well clear rather than motoring toward a pod.
animals.didYouKnow: The Cook Inlet beluga whale population is genetically distinct and federally endangered, numbering only a few hundred individuals.

animals.whereToLook: Den sites near lakeshores and open meadows
animals.viewingTip: If you spot a den, watch active fox behavior from well back with binoculars and never linger near the den entrance — repeated disturbance can cause a vixen to abandon a litter.
animals.didYouKnow: Red foxes in this region often shadow bears and eagles at salmon streams, scavenging scraps left behind.

animals.whereToLook: Mountain valleys along traditional migration corridors
animals.viewingTip: Watch migrating herds from a ridge or valley overlook with binoculars rather than moving toward the animals, which can split or stress a moving herd.
animals.didYouKnow: Some caribou herds that pass near Lake Clark migrate hundreds of miles seasonally between calving grounds and wintering areas.

animals.whereToLook: Remote backcountry drainages and alpine terrain
animals.viewingTip: A wolverine sighting is a matter of luck more than location; if you see one, stay still and observe from a distance with binoculars rather than trying to follow it.
animals.didYouKnow: Wolverines can range over hundreds of square miles, giving individual animals huge, thinly overlapping territories.
